_comment: Shared config for both halves of the pipeline. Secrets live in env vars or in the project .env, never here: ELEVENLABS_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

script._openrouter_model_note: Measured on 210 overflowing cues from one real episode, whole-episode prompt, effort medium. This model is a lottery, and that is fine because the losing ticket is detectable for free. Seven identical calls landed 207, 206, 205, 111, 93, 69 and 67 cues inside budget, and quality tracks how much the model bothered to think, visible in the reply before anyone reads the text: 513 reasoning tokens gave 93/210, 2338 gave 111/210, 5520 gave 207/210. So the stage validates and re-rolls (see accept_fit_ratio) instead of buying a steadier model. Rejected alternatives: luna-pro 207-208 but $0.017-0.021, and it is just luna at high effort under another name; gemini-3.5-flash burned 46000 reasoning tokens and returned TRUNCATED JSON on two runs out of three at $0.43 each; gemini-3.5-flash-lite ignores reasoning entirely (0 tokens) for a steady but mediocre 108-132/210 at $0.021; gemini-3.6-flash 196/210 at $0.196; gpt-5.6-terra 158/210 at $0.037.
script._accept_fit_ratio_note: Fraction of the overflowing cues that must come back inside their budget for a whole-episode reply to be accepted. Below it the call is re-rolled up to max_rerolls times, keeping the best reply seen. At roughly 40% good rolls this averages ~2.3 calls, about $0.014 an episode -- still cheaper than any model that is steady on the first try.
script._max_rerolls_note: Hard stop on re-rolling. After this the best reply so far is used and the shortfall is reported honestly rather than hidden; whatever still overflows gets sped up instead.
script._reuse_previous_note: Reuse condensed lines from <base>.condensed.json instead of redrawing them. The key is (cleaned source text, budget_chars, openrouter_model, reasoning_effort, hash of CONDENSE_SYSTEM), so any change to the prompt, the model, the effort, the cleaning rules or the merge gate misses on exactly the lines it really changed and on no others. Measured per episode: re-running the pipeline after an upstream change costs $0.71 without this and $0.09 with it ($4.27 a season against $0.54), and the TTS bill it also saves is 14-65x larger. Two honest caveats. First, whole-episode condensation sees the entire dialogue as context, so a reused line was written under a slightly different context than a fresh one would be -- the alternative is paying for the whole episode every time, and the line itself was accepted against the same budget. Second, a cue the model FAILED on is never stored, so it gets another chance on the next run instead of a cached failure. `script --redraw` ignores the file for one run; `reuse_previous: false` is the permanent version. Deleting the file buys exactly one clean draw, because the run that redraws also writes it again.
script._reasoning_effort_note: low is 3x cheaper but lands only 90/210 in budget; high costs 2x and adds nothing (206/210, 185 s). Send {"effort": ...} only -- {"enabled": false} is HTTP 400 on these models.
script._context_mode_note: The whole episode goes in one call: $0.196 vs $0.433 per episode against the same model batched, and every cue is shortened against the full dialogue instead of three neighbours. Cues to shorten are marked inline as '[id] >>> SKROC DO N ZNAKOW <<< text' and the model returns only those. This replaced the old batch_size/context_window knobs; max_prompt_chars is the only way back to batching, and only for an episode too long to fit one call.
script._temperature_note: Part of the measured winning call shape, not decoration: one whole-episode call with the same model and prompt landed 92/210 cues inside budget with the provider default and 206/210 at 0.3. Set it to null to send no temperature at all.
script._max_tokens_note: Reasoning effort is spent as a fraction of max_tokens, so omitting it starves the model: 62 reasoning tokens and 139/210 in budget without it, against 5000+ and 205/210 with it. 48000 covers 210 rewritten cues with room for thinking.
script._structured_outputs_note: Send response_format json_schema with strict true. OpenRouter routes to providers that support it, but enforcement is not guaranteed on every endpoint, so the reply is validated client-side regardless. If a provider refuses the schema outright the stage degrades to json_object for the rest of the run and says so.
script._retry_misses_note: After the first pass, cues that came back missing, empty, longer than the original or still over budget get ONE targeted second call that names them and the reason. Small prompt, small output, so it adds cents, not dollars.
script._max_prompt_chars_note: Above this the whole-episode prompt is split into contiguous segments (the batching fallback). A real 598-cue episode builds a 28 kB prompt, so this never triggers in practice; it exists so an absurdly long episode degrades instead of erroring.
script._measured_usd_per_episode_note: Reference figure for `cost` only, and only until an episode has really run. It must track openrouter_model AND the re-roll policy above, so it is the ~$0.014 an episode that luna averages at roughly 2.3 draws: a single clean draw of S02E01 (598 cues, 210 over budget) billed $0.0089, of which $0.0060 was the whole-episode call and $0.0029 the targeted retry. For comparison, the same episode through luna-pro in one draw billed $0.0233. Once <episode>.spend.json exists, `cost` reports what OpenRouter actually billed instead, read from usage.cost.
script._fallback_model_note: Used when openrouter_model has burned every re-roll and still missed accept_fit_ratio. Re-rolling a model that has drawn badly five times in a row is throwing good money after bad; terra is steadier per draw (158/210 at effort medium against luna's swing between 67 and 207) and costs about 4x, which is worth it only here. The best reply across every draw from both models wins, so escalating can never make the result worse.
script._fallback_rerolls_note: Extra draws from the fallback model beyond its first. Two attempts is the point of diminishing returns; past that the honest move is to accept and speed the stragglers up.
script._request_gap_ms_note: Minimum spacing between the starts of two OpenRouter calls, enforced process-wide alongside a hard cap of 3 concurrent calls. A single episode is already one call per draw, so this is not for the pipeline: it is for everything around it - benchmarks fanning several models out at once, or two runs of the same episode briefly overlapping - which from the provider's side is one account hammering it and shows up as requests queueing behind each other.

timing._duration_model_note: Fitted per voice by generating cues of every length and regressing duration on character count. Mateusz measures ms = 80 + 73.4 * chars, Bill measured 47 + 73.5, so the speaking rate is a property of the model rather than the voice and only the fixed cost moves. A flat chars_per_second misses that fixed part, and it dominates the short cues that make up half an episode. Most of it used to be dead air the engine pads on, which backends now trim. Re-fit when changing voice_id; set ms_per_char to 0 to fall back to the flat model.
timing._chars_per_second_note: Speaking rate of the chosen voice at speed=1.0. Run `lektor.py calibrate` to measure it for real; the measured value is cached per backend+voice+model in the work dir. What it actually drives is the ElevenLabs backend's per-line speed prediction. It reaches the character budgets ONLY through budget_for's 1000/cps fallback, i.e. with ms_per_char at 0; with ms_per_char set, calibrating changes no budget at all. Backends that control duration directly (piper) ignore it entirely.
timing._max_speed_note: Ceiling on voice_settings.speed. 1.2 is the API's own hard limit, verified: 1.25 comes back as invalid_voice_settings, "expected to be greater or equal to...". This is the engine genuinely reading faster, with its prosody intact, which is why it is the only time compression used.
timing._max_borrow_ms_note: How far a line may run past its own cue, into the silence that follows. Raised from 700 to 1500 because a real lektor routinely lags the picture and talks across the start of the next line; the borrow is still capped by the actual gap minus gap_guard_ms, so this only helps where there is real silence to take. Wider windows also mean less for the LLM to shorten, which makes the script stage cheaper as well as the delivery less rushed.
timing._budget_slack_note: Multiplier on the character budget handed to the LLM. 1.0 means the budget is exactly what fits at the voice's natural rate. It was briefly 1.18 to stop the model abbreviating, and that was the wrong lever: the extra room came back as fuller lines that overran their windows, 168 of them by 423 ms on average, and with atempo disabled that turns straight into the lektor lagging the picture. Abbreviations are a prompt problem and are fixed in the prompt; the budget stays honest.
timing._max_atempo_note: Post-hoc time stretch, DISABLED at 1.0 by owner decision after listening: atempo resamples finished speech and the artefacts are worse than an honestly faster reading. Anything that will not fit at max_speed is simply allowed to run long into the silence that follows, which is what a real lektor does anyway. Raise it only if that lag starts to matter more than the artefacts.
timing._number_slack_note: Extra budget for cues containing digits, on top of budget_slack. Spelling a number out multiplies its length - "14" becomes "czternascie" - so on an ordinary budget the model pays for the expansion by dropping a number, which defeats the point. Only a handful of cues per episode carry digits, so the lag this buys back is negligible.
timing._max_delay_ms_note: Ceiling on how far a line may be pushed later when the actor had not started speaking yet, and the switch for the whole feature: 0 disables it and the placement goes back to the card start. 600 ms because that is where a nudge stops being one. The score gate does not bound the lead on its own -- the worst lead passing it is +2526 ms, on a two-word cue the aligner guessed at -- so this cap is the thing that actually contains a bad anchor, and only 6 of 180 delays across the season are held by it. Re-timing every line to the acoustic onset was measured as a NET LOSS (-50.8 s of room, lines needing a speed-up 4 -> 41), so this is deliberately a nudge on a handful of lines and never a re-timing.
timing._delay_min_lead_ms_note: Smallest lead worth correcting. Below it the lektor is heard as being on the card, not ahead of it. Measured over all six episodes: 182 of 3443 lines lead by more than 300 ms, 35 by more than 500, 8 by more than 800.
timing._delay_keep_lead_ms_note: How much of the lead is kept rather than eaten. A card goes up a median 73 ms before the first word and that lead is working room, not error; a lektor starting exactly on the first syllable sounds late. So the delay closes the gap to this, never to zero.
timing._delay_min_score_note: Alignment confidence a card's onset must clear before anything is moved. Higher than the pause gate's 0.5 on purpose: a pause gate that acts on a bad alignment refuses a merge, a delay that acts on one moves a line that was never early. The +2003 ms leads reported by the ASR brief all sit below this.
timing._delay_match_tol_ms_note: How far apart a Polish card and its English counterpart may start and still be treated as the same card. The aligner reads the English track and the lektor is written from the Polish one; 3130 of 3443 cues start on a byte-identical timestamp and the rest are seconds away, so widening this to 200 ms buys 10 cues in 3443 and to 400 ms buys 28. It is a safety margin, not a search.
timing._speed_smooth_note: How far a speed-up bleeds into its neighbours, in seconds. A single line jumping to 1.2 while the ones around it sit at 1.0 is heard as the lektor suddenly hurrying; ramping the neighbours part of the way there makes the acceleration a gradient instead of a step. It also pays for itself: neighbours that finish earlier leave the crowded line more room, so it needs less speed-up than it did alone.
timing._speed_relax_note: Fraction of the computed excess speed actually applied, once the neighbours are sharing the load. 0.88 gives back about a fifth of a typical speed-up.

speech._comment: The `speech` stage: what the actors and the editor did, measured off the video, written to <base>.speech.json. Costs nothing and calls nothing paid. Everything it produces is optional - the merge gate degrades to today's text-only rules whenever a signal is missing.
speech._reference_srt_patterns_note: Where to find the English text the aligner is given, tried in order; {tag} is the S02E06 part of the filename, {base} the whole stem. English, because the acoustic model is English - WAV2VEC2_ASR_LARGE_LV60K_960H, which beat MMS_FA on this material 88 to 57 of 97 cues and is MIT rather than CC-BY-NC. Stream 3 first because it is the near-verbatim transcript: it keeps the 'Ooh', the stutters and the reaction sounds, so it transcribes what is uttered, while stream 2 is the cleaned reading version (3054 of ~3670 cue texts identical, 589 only in stream 3). The Polish track is never a candidate.
speech._centre_filter_note: The dialogue stem for free: on a 5.1 track the centre channel is where the voices are, so no source separation is needed - and none should be added, because the sibling yt-translator project MEASURED Demucs making alignment worse and dropped it, keeping exactly this band-pass. 120-7500 Hz is speech; dynaudnorm evens out the level so a whispered line aligns as well as a shouted one.
speech._downmix_filter_note: Fallback for a track that is not 5.1, where pan=mono|c0=FC has no centre channel to take. ffmpeg's own downmix is used instead and the artefact records which of the two ran, because a downmix carries the music and effects that the centre channel does not.
speech._min_score_note: Aligner confidence below which a cue contributes no word times at all. Not decoration: cues scoring under 0.35 were measured at 0.314 mean ASR token recall against 0.901 for cues at 0.7 and above, i.e. the low scorers are shouts over crowd noise where the times are guesses - and a guessed word time invents a silence that never happened, which is precisely what the pause gate would then act on. At 0.5, 475 of 616 cues on S02E06 qualify.
speech._fa_window_s_note: How much contiguous cue text is aligned in one pass. Measured against 120 s windows on a real episode: better scores (475 vs 393 of 616 cues), 2.6x less VRAM, 1.9x faster, and the two agree to 10 ms at the median. Do NOT drop to per-cue windows with a short pad: without a <star> token the aligner drags a cue's first word backwards onto whatever speech sits in the pad, fabricating the exact statistic this artefact exists to measure.
speech._store_min_gap_note: Shortest silence written into the artefact. Half of merge_min_pause_ms, so the threshold can be lowered in config and re-measured without re-running the GPU; below that it is inter-word coarticulation, not a pause, and it would double the file for nothing.
speech._scene_threshold_note: ffmpeg's own scene score above which a frame is a new shot. 0.35 yields 433 cuts on S02E06 at a median shot of 2.59 s, which is normal for single-camera comedy; it costs about 60 s of CPU for a 35-minute 1080p episode and reads the video without writing anything back.
speech._asr_container_note: The container forced alignment runs INSIDE, by name. It is borrowed, not owned: it belongs to ~/projects/yt-translator, it holds a resident faster-whisper large-v3, and this stage neither calls its HTTP API nor writes into its source tree. It uses only the torchaudio 2.6 that is already installed there, which is why nothing has to be installed anywhere and why the torch pin must not be disturbed. One scratch directory under the container's /tmp is created and removed again. If the container is down, the stage says so and writes an artefact with shot cuts only.
speech._tmp_dir_note: Where the 16 kHz mono extract lands, about 67 MB per episode, deleted when the stage finishes. Empty means the system temp. Point it at fast local disk if the work dir is on a network or 9p mount, where writing that file is far slower than reading the video it came from.
speech._timeouts_note: Ceilings, not expectations. Measured on S02E06: 18 s to extract the audio, 9 s to align 616 cues (234x realtime), 58 s for the shot cuts. These exist so a wedged container or an unreadable file becomes an error instead of a hang.

voice._backend_note: elevenlabs | piper | chatterbox. elevenlabs costs money and sounds like broadcast; piper is free, runs on CPU and hits its time windows exactly, measured on a real 598-cue episode at 19.7 s cold and 0.7 s once the cache is warm, 597 of the 598 lines inside their window; chatterbox is free and can clone a voice from a reference clip, but it needs the GPU and runs at RTF ~1.6 against piper's 0.064, so an episode takes hours instead of minutes. Override for a single run with `--backend`.
voice._concurrency_note: Default parallel TTS calls. ElevenLabs caps this per plan. Flash/Turbo: Free 4, Starter 6, Creator 10, Pro 20, Scale/Business 30. Other models: Free 2, Starter 3, Creator 5, Pro 10, Scale/Business 15. 8 leaves headroom under the Creator/Flash cap of 10. A backend may override it in its own sub-table.

elevenlabs._voice_id_note: Mateusz - Polish Legend Narrator, a low calm baritone from the shared library. Chosen by ear from ten candidates read over the same 150 s of S02E03, a window picked for English names and lines that invite acting. Replaced Bill pqHfZKP75CvOlQylNhV4, which was fine at first and wore thin: a lektor has to be transparent, and the test is whether you stop noticing him. Comparison clips are in <input_dir>/_lektor/glosy/.
elevenlabs._model_id_note: eleven_flash_v2_5 is flat, cheap ($0.05/1000 chars) and gets 2x the concurrency; eleven_multilingual_v2 and eleven_v3 are warmer at $0.10/1000 chars. Compare them with `lektor.py sample`.
elevenlabs._output_format_note: Must stay in the mp3_* or opus_* family: the cache is decoded with `ffmpeg -i pipe:0`, which cannot read headerless PCM. mp3_44100_192 needs Creator or better.
elevenlabs._speed_max_note: Hard API limit on voice_settings.speed, documented as 0.7-1.2. Anything above it is rejected, so this clamps timing.max_speed; what does not fit at 1.2 is stretched locally with atempo, which is free.
elevenlabs._max_retries_note: Attempts per line against 429/500/502/503 only. 401, 402 and 422 mean the same thing every time and surface at once instead of sleeping five times.
elevenlabs._settings_note: voice_settings sent with every call. speed is NOT here: it is computed per line from the measured chars/second and clamped by speed_max. style above 0 makes a lektor act, which is the one thing he must not do. stability was 0.6 here and 1.0 in the renderer that actually produced all six episodes -- the config was simply wrong, and every line on disk is keyed on 1.0. At 1.0 the voice stops acting, which is the whole point of the profile.
elevenlabs._send_neighbour_text_note: Send previous_text / next_text with every line, so the engine reads it as part of a continuous delivery instead of as an isolated sentence. Free in API cost, and part of the cache key: turning it off re-reads the whole episode.
elevenlabs._speed_plan_note: 'neighbour_smoothed' plans every line's speed over the whole episode, spreading a crowded line's speed-up across its neighbours (timing.speed_smooth_s, timing.speed_relax). 'per_line' asks each line to fit its own window alone, which is heard as the lektor suddenly hurrying and then stopping. Smoothed is what shipped.

piper._voice_note: Downloaded from rhasspy/piper-voices on first use. The Polish shelf is pl_PL-darkman-medium (male, flat, unexpressive - the lektor profile), pl_PL-bass-high (male, high tier, ~3x slower to synthesise), pl_PL-mc_speech-medium (male, clipped and clerical), pl_PL-gosia-medium (female) and pl_PL-mls_6892-low (male, audibly rough). All single-speaker, all 22050 Hz.
piper._voice_dir_note: Where the .onnx and its .onnx.json are kept. Outside the work dir on purpose: the voice is 63 MB and is shared by every show, while the work dir belongs to one release. A half-written download is deleted rather than left behind, because piper skips re-downloading any file that already exists and is non-empty.
piper._model_path_note: Overrides voice/voice_dir with an explicit path to an .onnx (its .onnx.json must sit next to it). Empty means use the downloaded voice.
piper._speaker_note: Speaker id inside a multi-speaker model. Every pl_PL voice on the shelf is single-speaker, so 0 means 'the voice's own default' and there is nothing else to pick.
piper._length_scale_note: Piper's direct duration knob: larger is slower, and it doubles as the search ceiling because a lektor is only ever asked to hurry. 1.0 is the voice's natural rate; lines that already fit are spoken at it and never touched again.
piper._noise_scale_note: Acoustic sampling noise, the model's own default. It colours the timbre, not the length, so it is safe to move; noise_w_scale is the one that must stay at 0.
piper._noise_w_scale_note: The stochastic duration predictor, and the reason the search is exact. At the model default of 0.8 the same text at the same length_scale measured 4783-5050 ms across eight runs, 5.4% of jitter against a 60 ms tolerance; at 0.0 the duration is bit-exact reproducible. It also flattens the prosody, which is the lektor profile anyway.
piper._search_min_note: Floor of the length_scale search, i.e. how fast this voice may be pushed: 0.6 is about 1.67x the natural rate and is already at the edge of what stays intelligible. A line that does not fit even here is handed back at the clamp and reported as clamped rather than silently overrun; on the real 598-cue episode that was 4 lines, worst overrun +16%. Those are the condensation stage's problem, not the voice stage's.
piper._search_max_note: Ceiling of the search, only ever reached through length_scale itself: the search starts at length_scale and moves down, because a lektor is asked to hurry and never to dawdle. It exists to keep an edited config from asking for a two-minute reading of a two-second cue.
piper._search_iterations_note: Probes allowed after the first, natural-rate reading. Measured over the real 598-cue episode: 2.24 syntheses per cue overall, 374 cues fitting on the first reading and never probed at all, 224 shortened to within 1.1% of their window at the median.
piper._tolerance_ms_note: How far under the window counts as landed. It cannot be met exactly on short cues - phoneme lengths are rounded to whole decoder frames, so a 30-character cue moves in 20-80 ms steps - and the search stops on its own once the bracket is finer than the steps. Undershoot is harmless anyway: the leftover is silence between lines, and the search always returns the SLOWEST rate that still fits.
piper._threads_note: onnxruntime intra-op threads PER UTTERANCE, deliberately 1. Measured over 150 real cues: auto (16) threads x 1 worker = 9.9 cues/s, 1 thread x 16 workers = 35.2 cues/s. These clips are 1-4 s long, so onnxruntime's pool spends its time synchronising. CPU only: CUDA renders an episode in 136.5 s against CPU's 138.4 s and has already failed once with an onnxruntime EP error, so there is no GPU switch here. Do not add onnxruntime-gpu.
piper._concurrency_note: Worker threads over one shared session, measured: 4 -> 20.6 cues/s, 8 -> 30.1, 12 -> 34.7, 16 -> 35.2, 20 -> 32.6. It plateaus at the core count and degrades past it. Parallel output was verified bit-for-bit identical to serial.

chatterbox._venv_note: python 3.11 with torch and chatterbox already installed. Reuse it; do not reinstall. The pipeline itself runs on python 3.13 and has no torch, so the model is held by a worker subprocess launched from this venv and spoken to over a JSON pipe.
chatterbox._dtype_note: bfloat16 | float32. THIS IS THE FIX FOR BOTH RECORDED CRASHES, do not set float16. T3's CFG combine and the temperature divide push logits past the float16 ceiling; they saturate to inf, softmax turns that into nan and torch.multinomial raises a device-side assert that poisons the CUDA context for the rest of the process. Measured on a 24-generation grid over temperature 0.5-1.0 x cfg_weight 0.3-0.7: float16 died on generation 1, bfloat16 passed 24/24 at 2607 MiB, float32 passed at 3716 MiB and is about 12% faster. bfloat16 is the default because it fits even the ~2.6 GiB budget WDDM hands a WSL2 process on a busy desktop. float16 is refused with a named error rather than silently accepted.
chatterbox._language_id_note: Language tag for the multilingual model, passed straight to generate(). It selects the grapheme set, so a Polish script read under another tag comes out mispronounced rather than merely accented.
chatterbox._reference_wav_note: Voice cloning reference; empty means the model's builtin speaker. Cloning WORKS once dtype is not float16 - the old failure was 'mat1 and mat2 must have the same dtype, but got Float and Half', because prepare_conditionals builds float32 conditionals and float16 weights refuse them, and the backend now casts them at T3's entry point. Verified with the model's own voice encoder: a cloned clip sits at cosine 0.82-0.85 to the reference against 0.63-0.67 for the builtin voice. Give it a clean single-speaker clip of 8-20 s; container and sample rate do not matter because librosa resamples. The clone copies the reference's LOUDNESS too, so a quiet reference makes quiet speech - harmless, since the mix stage normalises the voice against the programme.
chatterbox._exaggeration_note: Emotional intensity. A lektor is deliberately flat, so leave it at the neutral 0.5; it also changes nothing about duration.
chatterbox._cfg_weight_note: Classifier-free-guidance weight, how hard the model is pushed toward the text. 0.3-0.7 were all stable in bfloat16. It is one of the two knobs that overflowed float16, so raising it on float16 is the fastest way back to the CUDA assert.
chatterbox._temperature_note: Sampling temperature. 0.5, 0.65, 0.7, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.3 all generated cleanly in bfloat16; the crash blamed on temperature was the float16 overflow, which the divide by a temperature below 1.0 merely made likelier.
chatterbox._seed_note: Only re-rolls takes. The per-line seed is derived from the cache key, so the same text under the same settings always yields the same reading; change this to get a different one.
chatterbox._load_timeout_s_note: How long the ready handshake may take. It covers snapshot_download plus a warmup generation, measured at 11-45 s once the model is in the HF cache and minutes on the very first run, which is why it is this generous.
chatterbox._render_timeout_s_note: Ceiling on one line. Generation is bounded by max_new_tokens=1000 at roughly 24 tokens/s, so this is far above anything real and exists only to turn a hung worker into an error instead of a hang.
chatterbox._concurrency_note: Fixed at 1; the backend ignores any other value. One model on one GPU behind one worker process with one request/response pipe, 2607 MiB resident, RTF ~1.6. Extra threads would only queue on that pipe.

mix._channel_layout_note: Layout of the finished track: '5.1(side)' or 'stereo'. 5.1 is what ships -- the lektor lands on the centre channel, where dialogue lives and where a stereo downmix folds it evenly into both speakers, and every other channel keeps its own material. Stereo is the fallback for a source that has no surround track; the mix then carries the voice on both channels. The layout also picks the encode profile below.
mix._voice_channels_note: Output channels the lektor is laid onto, in ffmpeg's 5.1(side) order FL FR FC LFE SL SR. [2] is FC. Ignored in stereo, where the lektor is laid on both channels at full level -- which is why voice_channel_comp_db is 0 there: two correlated channels already sum the 3 dB the centre-only case has to buy back.
mix._voice_channel_comp_db_note: Level compensation for putting the voice on ONE channel instead of two. Every level in this mix was tuned against a stereo fold, where L and R sum 3 dB; the centre channel alone does not, so without this the lektor lands 3 dB quieter than the number voice_over_program_db promises. It is a correction, not a taste knob -- voice_over_program_db is the taste knob.
mix._level_reference_note: How the programme's own loudness is measured, and every level in the mix hangs off it. 'stereo_fold' downmixes the source to two channels first, which is what the mix was tuned against; 'as_is' measures whatever channels the source has, and on a 5.1 source the LFE and the surrounds move the number enough to unbalance the whole thing.
mix._levels_note: Every level is relative to the programme's own measured loudness, never to dBFS. The first cut used an absolute voice_target_dbfs of -18 and buried a quiet film under a lektor 25 dB above it; the same setting would have been too quiet on a loud one. All three numbers below were then set by ear on a real scene.
mix._voice_over_program_db_note: Lektor RMS above the programme RMS. 8 was judged slightly too strong and 5 slightly too weak.
mix._duck_to_db_note: Where the original sits while the lektor speaks, relative to its natural level. Deeper than about -10 starts erasing the scene instead of making room in it.
mix._program_gain_db_note: Makeup applied to the original in the gaps. The source is quiet, and a lektor track should not make the film quieter than watching it without one.
mix._limiter_note: The limiter is sample-accurate: instantaneous attack, one-pole release over limiter_release_ms, and the reduction is carried across the 10 s encode blocks so a peak never steps the gain at a block seam. A peak therefore pulls down its own neighbourhood and nothing else. Shorter releases recover faster and pump more; 120 ms is long enough to hold a reduction across a syllable and short enough to be back before the next line.
mix._hold_ms_note: Keep the original ducked through any gap shorter than this instead of letting it climb back and drop again. Measured without it on one episode: 324 full recoveries, 198 of them under a second, the programme swinging 11 dB at up to 52 dB/s between neighbouring lines. That pumping is what a listener hears as the film being chopped; holding through the short gaps removes it and costs only the brief moments of original audio nobody was going to hear anyway.
mix._release_ms_note: How slowly the original climbs back once the lektor really has finished. Slower than the attack on purpose, and slower still since hold_ms landed, because every remaining recovery is now a real one and should feel gradual.
mix._voice_presence_note: High shelf on the lektor, matched by measurement rather than taste. Two voices at the same loudness are not equally present: band by band at equal RMS, Mateusz had 3.6 dB less above 4 kHz than Bill, where consonants live, and that reads as further away and quieter. A shelf of 6 dB at 4 kHz puts his 4-8 kHz band at 57.6 against Bill's 57.5, so the two are interchangeable in tone. Re-measure when changing voice_id; turning the fader up instead only makes the mud louder.
mix._voice_trim_note: Per-voice level nudge on top of voice_over_program_db, for when the tone is right and the balance still is not. Cheap to retune: the speech is cached, so only the mix is rebuilt.
mix._duck_mode_note: broadband turns the whole programme down under the lektor; spectral turns down only the band the voice actually occupies and leaves the bass and the air alone. The second is what a multiband sidechain does in a studio (FabFilter Pro-MB, sonible smart:comp, TrackSpacer): music keeps its weight and sparkle, the midrange makes room, and because the whole spectrum is not moving there is far less to hear as pumping. Masking happens in the midrange, so ducking the rest was paying with impact for nothing.
mix._duck_band_note: The band the lektor competes for. Below it is weight and above it is air, neither of which masks speech. Split with a Linkwitz-Riley crossover (ffmpeg acrossover) because the two halves must sum back to the original when their gains are equal; band-passing the middle and calling the difference the rest does NOT work, since an IIR band-pass shifts phase and the difference still carries the midrange at full level. That shortcut measured 6.8 dB LOUDER in the speech band than broadband ducking, the opposite of the intent.
mix._duck_mid_note: How far the speech band drops under the lektor in spectral mode. Deeper than it was: the first cut sat at -11 and the lektor still blended into the bed, and this is the only band being touched.
mix._duck_rest_note: Bass and air under the lektor. Barely moved, so the film keeps its weight - but no longer untouched, because at 1.5 dB a loud passage still crowded the voice.
mix._pre_roll_ms_note: How long before the lektor speaks the duck begins. Measured at the old 250 ms with a 180 ms attack, the bed was still only 4.5 dB down when the voice arrived - 6.5 dB short of its target - and did not reach depth until half a second INTO the line. That is heard as two people talking at once, which is exactly what it was.
mix._attack_ms_note: Time constant of the duck going down. Short, because the pre-roll only helps if the fall completes inside it.
mix._pause_note: Internal pauses the engine inserts, mostly at commas. Measured over 476 of them: median 180 ms, p75 320, p90 510, max 700, and a line with two commas spends 23% of its length not speaking. pause_ratio is how much of each pause ABOVE pause_floor_ms survives - 1.0 leaves them alone. The floor is where a gap stops being heard as a pause and reads as articulation, so it is never taken; only the excess is compressed, which keeps a sentence boundary longer than a comma instead of flattening both to the same length the way a flat scaling would.

encode._note: The STEREO profile. AC3 muxes into MKV and plays on everything, including dumb TVs. Set codec/extension to flac for a lossless handoff at ~3x the size.
encode._surround_note: Used when mix.channel_layout is a surround layout. E-AC-3 at 768k is what produced every episode on disk; ac3 at 256k cannot carry six channels credibly, so the profile is chosen by layout rather than shared.

clean._strip_note: Markup, HI tags and parentheticals. Bracket stripping also removes on-screen-text glosses, which lektor does not read.
clean._pronunciation_note: Foreign names respelled the way a Polish voice must say them. Keep this list SHORT: the multilingual voice already reads English names correctly, and respelling those only breaks them. It is for names whose language is neither Polish nor English, where the voice falls back on Polish letter rules - Spanish 'Rojas' comes out 'royas' instead of 'Rohas'. Keys match on the STEM and the case ending follows automatically (Rojasa -> Rohasa, Rojasowi -> Rohasowi), so add the nominative only. This runs on EVERY cue, before budgets and before the LLM, unlike condensation which only touches cues that do not fit. Extend it by ear, per show.
clean._skip_patterns_note: A cue matching any of these never reaches the lektor at all. The note characters mark sung lyrics, which a lektor does not read over - the song is the scene. The pattern deliberately matches a note ANYWHERE, not the opening-and-closing pair it used to: '♪TRENERNATE - #AFCRICHMOND #WONDERKID' opens with one and never closes it, and slipped through to be read aloud.
clean._spoken_symbols_note: Symbols rewritten into the words a lektor actually says, applied to EVERY cue before budgets and before the LLM. Same reasoning as the pronunciation table: a short cue never goes to the model, so a '#' left in it would be read as whatever the voice makes of the glyph. The LLM handles digits; these are the marks it has no rule for.
clean._merge_gap_note: Two cards are joined only when BOTH hold: the gap is no larger than this, and the first card does not finish its sentence. The gap alone proves nothing - this release puts a fixed 82-85 ms between every card, 55% of all gaps, and the next distinct value is 417 ms. Merging on the gap alone glued two finished sentences 89% of the time, including across shot changes, across speaker turns and onto on-screen title cards. Set to 0 to switch merging off.
clean._merge_gate_note: OFF, by listening, against the measurement that motivated it. The evidence was solid: half of all merges join across a pause the actors really took or a shot cut, 117 of 231 seams over six episodes. The conclusion drawn from it was wrong. Judged on 22 A/B pairs rendered both ways over the real audio with everything else held identical, merging won decisively - splitting a sentence at its comma, which is exactly where actors pause, made the lektor sound like it was reading word by word. A lektor is a narrator reading a text, not a performer imitating a delivery: he reads the sentence, and the pause in the picture is not his to copy. Set to 'pause', 'cut' or 'both' to re-enable; the speech.json artefact stays useful regardless, since the per-line delay job needs its onsets.
clean._merge_min_pause_note: Shortest silence in the delivery that counts as the actors having paused. 300 ms is the threshold the effect was measured at, not one derived from a distribution, and it is the single knob that matters: across six episodes it takes the 211 text-rule merges to 95 at 200 ms, 124 at 300, 162 at 500 and 190 at 800. It is the honest place for a second opinion by ear, which is the only test that can settle it - the median silence sitting on a merge seam is 520 ms, comfortably above the threshold either way.
clean._merge_max_pause_note: Longest silence still read as a pause. Past this it is a stretch the aligner never covered - a scene with no subtitled speech in it - not a breath inside one sentence, and a hole in the evidence must not masquerade as evidence. MEASURED over six episodes: 118 merge seams have a silence of at least 300 ms on them, and 13 of those silences run 5.2, 6.4, 6.4, 11.2, 11.8, 11.8, 13.8, 25.9, 25.9, 25.9, 26.3, 27.0 and 51.0 SECONDS. A 51-second pause between two cards that are 83 ms apart and both carry dialogue is not something an actor did. The other 105 have a median of 520 ms. This cap is the only place this implementation is deliberately more conservative than the simulation the feature was designed from: uncapped, S02E06 reproduces that simulation almost exactly (570 cues, 22 merges, 246 over budget, 2148 chars of deficit against a predicted 571 / 21 / 247 / 2145); capped it keeps 7 more merges an episode that the simulation threw away on missing evidence.
clean._merge_pause_tol_note: How far outside the 83 ms seam that silence may sit and still be about the seam. The alignment's own onset error against the card is p50 90 ms and p90 293 ms, so a tolerance below about 150 ms would start missing real pauses through timing noise alone, and one much larger would start catching the pause after the NEXT word. It is a weak knob and that is reassuring: over six episodes the merges land at 134 with no tolerance at all, 130 at 100 ms, 124 at 250 and 118 at 500, i.e. the signal is not an artefact of where the window is drawn.
clean._merge_cut_pad_note: Widen the seam before looking for a shot cut. Zero because the seam is already the whole interval between the two cards and a cut inside it is unambiguous; padding trades a rare missed cut for refusing merges over cuts that happen mid-card, which is a different question.
clean._merge_limits_note: Guards on a merged utterance. Looser than the first attempt because the predicate is now narrow: with the old timestamp-only rule a 7 s cap chopped 571 of 1926 candidate joins, and 87 of those refusals landed mid-sentence - moving the hole rather than closing it.

units._currency_note: Amounts written the English way are said the Polish way: the symbol comes first on the page and the number comes first in the mouth, so $10 is dziesiec dolarow and never dolar dziesiec. The VALUE is never converted - exchange rates move and a lektor quoting an old sum in todays zloty would be stating a falsehood. A three-digit group after the separator is read as thousands, one or two digits as cents.

clean._units_note: Imperial measurements rewritten as metric. Deliberately narrow: mined over 26950 Polish subtitle lines from 44 films, a plain unit-name regex found 22 matches of which TWO were measurements. 'stopa' was a body part 12 times out of 12, 'funt' was pounds sterling 4 out of 4, and 'cali' was the adjective 'cały' - 'Wszyscy cali i zdrowi' would have become 'Wszyscy 2,54 cm i zdrowi'. So a unit converts ONLY when a numeral stands immediately in front of it and the line matches no idiom. 'pound' and 'ounce' are OFF by default because in British material a pound is money; enable them per show if the English track confirms mass. tolerance is how far a value may be moved to land on something a person would say - six feet becomes 1,8 m rather than 1,8288. A source written with decimals is treated as deliberate precision and is not snapped.
